answer.label: Not a verbatim quote — a modern paraphrase of Xenophon’s Socrates
answer.authorDates: c. 470–399 BC · Athenian philosopher, as reported by Xenophon
answer.sourceLine: The thought is genuinely Socratic, but no one is recorded saying these exact words. The line descends from Xenophon’s Memorabilia (Book II, ch. 6), where Socrates tells Critobulus that “the shortest and surest way to live with honour in the world is to be in reality what we would appear to be” — Edward Bysshe’s 1712 English rendering. Quote sites trimmed “shortest and surest” to “greatest” and swapped “be in reality what we would appear to be” for the snappier “be what we pretend to be,” a phrasing that appears in no actual translation.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: Book II, ch. 6 — Socrates to Critobulus (Memorabilia II.6.39)

source.excerpt: … the shortest and surest way to live with honour in the world is to be in reality what we would appear to be: and if you observe, you will find that all human virtues increase and strengthen themselves by the practice and experience of them.
trail: Edward Bysshe’s 1712 translation of Xenophon carries the genuine line: Socrates tells Critobulus “the shortest and surest way to live with honour in the world is to be in reality what we would appear to be” (Project Gutenberg).
Quote sites recast it as “the greatest way to live with honor in this world is to be what we pretend to be” and pin it on Socrates — a wording in no real translation (Goodreads).
The ‘pretend to be’ phrasing echoes a genuinely different author: Kurt Vonnegut’s “We are what we pretend to be…” from Mother Night (Wikiquote).
Cicero preserves the same Socratic maxim — “strive to be what you wish to be thought to be” — in De Officiis II.43 (Perseus).
source.excerptNote: Bysshe’s 1712 translation of Xenophon. The popular version replaces “shortest and surest” with “greatest” and “be in reality what we would appear to be” with “be what we pretend to be” — neither is in the original.

source.rightsNote: The genuine line comes from Xenophon’s ancient Greek Memorabilia (long in the public domain) in Edward Bysshe’s 1712 English translation, itself well out of copyright. The specific popular wording — “be what we pretend to be” — is an anonymous modern paraphrase that appears in no identifiable published source, so no clean rights status attaches to it.

author.bio: Socrates (c. 470–399 BC) was an Athenian philosopher who wrote nothing himself; everything we have of him comes through his students, chiefly Xenophon and Plato. Xenophon’s Memorabilia preserves his plain, practical ethics — including the maxim that the surest road to honour is not to seem good but actually to become what you wish to appear.

misattribution.heading: How this quote goes wrong
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Socrates is roughly fair — the thought is his, via Xenophon — but the exact words are not. Two things get muddled here:

items.why: No translation of Xenophon — or any classical text — renders the line as “be what we pretend to be.” The genuine 1712 wording is “be in reality what we would appear to be” (Project Gutenberg).

Vonnegut really did write “We are what we pretend to be, so we must be careful about what we pretend to be” in Mother Night — a separate, correctly-his quote whose phrasing likely contaminated the Socrates paraphrase (Wikiquote).

misattribution.truthLine: The real Socratic line is Xenophon’s: “the shortest and surest way to live with honour in the world is to be in reality what we would appear to be” (Memorabilia II.6, Bysshe trans.).

context.heading: The idea behind the line
lead: Xenophon’s Socrates is coaching young Critobulus on how to win real friends and a real reputation. His point is blunt: don’t chase the appearance of virtue, because a false reputation collapses the instant you’re asked to deliver on it. The safest road to honour is simply to become good at the thing you want to be admired for.

The modern ‘pretend to be’ rewrite keeps the shape of that idea but nudges its spirit — from ‘be genuinely what you appear’ toward ‘live up to your pretense.’ It’s a memorable line, but it is Xenophon’s Socrates filtered through an 18th-century translator and then smoothed by the internet, not anything Socrates is recorded as saying word-for-word.
context.pull: “Be in reality what we would appear to be” — not “pretend to be.”
